correlates.name: First-Dose Effect (Alpha Blocker Orthostatic Hypotension)
correlates.presentation: dizziness or syncope on standing, most prominent with the first dose or a dose increase; it tends to subside as blood pressure normalizes but may persist.
correlates.pathophysiology: loss of alpha-1 mediated venoconstriction on standing lets blood pool in the legs, so cerebral perfusion falls (Slide 11).
correlates.treatment: make the first dose small and give it at bedtime so the peak concentration falls during sleep; add a diuretic to counter the sodium and water retention.

correlates.name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
correlates.pathophysiology: alpha-1 receptors in the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate hold the outlet constricted.
correlates.treatment: an alpha-1 blocker relaxes that smooth muscle and improves urine flow (Slide 12).

correlates.name: Pheochromocytoma
correlates.presentation: hypertension and sweating from excessive catecholamine release.
correlates.pathophysiology: a tumor of the adrenal medulla secreting norepinephrine (mainly) and epinephrine, episodically or continuously.
correlates.treatment: phenoxybenzamine perioperatively; because it is an irreversible blocker the blockade outlasts the drug (duration >=3 days). Surgery is definitive.

correlates.name: Hypertension in Pregnancy
correlates.treatment: methyldopa for chronic management (Slide 20); hydralazine, including intravenously, for hypertensive emergency during pregnancy or postpartum (Slide 30).

correlates.name: Clonidine Withdrawal (Rebound Hypertension)
correlates.presentation: rebound hypertension with headache, apprehension, tremors, abdominal pain, sweating and tachycardia - a catalogue of sympathetic effects.
correlates.pathophysiology: sympathetic outflow has been suppressed for months. Abrupt discontinuation releases a catecholamine surge (Slide 21).

correlates.name: Hydralazine-Induced Lupus-Like Syndrome
correlates.presentation: rash (the malar butterfly distribution, Slide 33), arthralgia, myalgia and fever.
correlates.pathophysiology: hydralazine is inactivated by N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2). Slow acetylators carry polymorphisms giving fewer or less active enzymes, so plasma levels run high for a given dose (Slide 25).
correlates.treatment: reversible - it resolves when the drug is withdrawn.

correlates.name: Nitroprusside Cyanide Toxicity
correlates.pathophysiology: cyanide is part of the nitroprusside molecule, released when red blood cells take the drug up. Detoxification by rhodanese needs a sulfur donor and saturates; a large or prolonged infusion exhausts the sulfur supply and cyanide accumulates (Slide 24).
correlates.treatment: two antidote strategies (Slide 32) - sodium nitrite followed by sodium thiosulfate, supplying the sulfur donor that lets cyanide metabolism continue; or hydroxocobalamin, which binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, nontoxic vitamin B12.

drugs.name: Prazosin
drugs.mechanism: Selective alpha-1 antagonism relaxing both resistance arterioles and capacitance veins, so preload falls along with peripheral vascular resistance
drugs.indication: Add-on therapy for mild to moderate refractory hypertension; not initial therapy because it offers less cardiovascular mortality protection
drugs.adverseEffects: First-dose orthostatic hypotension and syncope, worst at initiation or dose increase; give a small first dose at bedtime

drugs.name: Terazosin
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 selective blockade with near-100% bioavailability and a 12-hour half-life supporting once-daily dosing
drugs.indication: Hypertension with benign prostatic hyperplasia, where relaxing bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle improves urine flow
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, nasal stuffiness from loss of mucosal vasoconstriction, and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome

drugs.name: Doxazosin
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-1 selective blockade cleared by CYP3A4 with a 22-hour half-life and over 24 hours of action
drugs.indication: Once-daily therapy for hypertension with coexisting BPH
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, compensatory sodium and water retention that calls for a companion diuretic, and floppy iris syndrome

drugs.name: Phenoxybenzamine
drugs.mechanism: Irreversible non-selective alpha blockade favoring alpha-1 over alpha-2, so recovery requires synthesis of new receptors
drugs.indication: Pheochromocytoma — pre-operative alpha blockade before any beta blocker is added — and urinary outlet obstruction
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia from alpha-2 autoreceptor block releasing unregulated norepinephrine, miosis, and 3 or more days of effect after a dose

drugs.name: Phentolamine
drugs.mechanism: Competitive non-selective alpha blockade with equal alpha-1 and alpha-2 affinity, given intravenously with a 19-minute half-life
drugs.indication: Vasopressor extravasation, and reversal of the vasoconstrictor in dental local anesthesia
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked reflex tachycardia and hypotension over its 10-30 minute duration

drugs.name: Clonidine
drugs.mechanism: Alpha-2 agonism at brainstem receptors — postsynaptic alpha-2 inhibits sympathetic neurons while presynaptic alpha-2 cuts norepinephrine release — lowering sympathetic and raising parasympathetic tone while preserving baroreceptor sensitivity, renal blood flow and GFR
drugs.indication: Refractory hypertension after ACE inhibitor, diuretic and CCB; also epidural pain control, ADHD, opioid and alcohol withdrawal, and menopausal vasomotor symptoms
drugs.adverseEffects: Sedation, dry mouth, constipation and bradycardia; abrupt cessation gives a catecholamine surge with rebound hypertension, so the beta blocker must be tapered off several days first

drugs.name: Methyldopa
drugs.mechanism: Converted by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a false transmitter that replaces norepinephrine in vesicles and acts on alpha-2 receptors
drugs.indication: Hypertension in pregnancy — the long-standing agent of choice
drugs.adverseEffects: Sedation and depression; onset takes 4-6 hours but the effect lasts 24-48 hours

drugs.name: Hydralazine
drugs.mechanism: Relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle only, by a mechanism that has never been defined; it undergoes NAT2 acetylation, so effect varies with acetylator status
drugs.indication: Moderate to severe hypertension, HFrEF paired with isosorbide dinitrate, and hypertensive emergency in pregnancy or postpartum
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia plus salt and water retention — because veins are untouched — so it needs a beta blocker and a diuretic alongside

drugs.name: Minoxidil
drugs.mechanism: Its active metabolite minoxidil sulfate opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing arteriolar smooth muscle so it cannot contract
drugs.indication: Severe hypertension as a last-line agent, with a very strong antihypertensive effect lasting about 3 days
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked reflex tachycardia and fluid retention requiring a beta blocker and loop diuretic, plus hypertrichosis and pericardial effusion

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.mechanism: Taken up by red cells and split into nitric oxide and cyanide; the nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP, dilating arteries and veins alike
drugs.indication: Acute severe hypertension, acute decompensated heart failure, and controlled hypotension during surgery — onset under 2 minutes, duration 1-10 minutes
drugs.adverseEffects: Cyanide and thiocyanate accumulation, since detoxification by rhodanese is saturable and thiocyanate clearance takes about 3 days, longer still in renal failure

drugs.name: Fenoldopam
drugs.mechanism: Dopamine D1 receptor agonism coupled through Gs to adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, dilating peripheral arterioles while producing natriuresis and diuresis
drugs.indication: Severe hypertension for up to 48 hours, particularly useful when renal function is compromised and in pediatric patients
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia, headache and flushing; a 5-minute half-life makes it fully titratable

transporters.name: K-ATP Channel (vascular smooth muscle)
transporters.location: Plasma membrane of arteriolar smooth muscle cells
transporters.function: Opening it lets potassium leave, hyperpolarizing the cell so voltage-gated calcium channels stay shut and the arteriole cannot contract
transporters.regulation: Opened by minoxidil sulfate, the active metabolite of minoxidil; closed by sulfonylureas in the pancreatic beta cell isoform
transporters.inhibitor: Sulfonylureas act on the beta-cell isoform; the vascular channel is opened, not blocked, by minoxidil
